author: jannik031153
content:
Very cool <@624174437821972480> , the dashboard is great! Couple of questions/comments:
- How do you handle multiple transactions in one sandwich?
- How do you calculate the attacker profit if the backrun does not fully undo the frontrun?
- Do you have a feeling how conservative the estimate is, in particular are you aware of more involved strategies that are not detected, maybe e.g. combined sandwich/arbitrage trades?
- Attacker gross profit and average profit per attack might be interesting to see from the victim's perspective as well (I assume they're not quite the same numbers because of DEX and tx fee inefficiencies). Also, for the average attack, the percentage of the trade volume is probably more relevant to users than the absolute amount.
- Do you see which pools are affected the most? Smaller pools will have higher slippage, but at the same time there's fewer trades in them, maybe diagram pool size vs extracted value could be interesting. 
- Percentage of attacked trades could be interesting too (not sure if count or volume)
- Maybe a way to cross check the detection could be to look at the execution price relative to the slippage tolerance. If a transaction executes at the worst allowed price it most likely got sandwiched.

author: dhanush0512
content:
Thanks @Jannik, this is genuinely great feedback. Going through each one:

**1. Multiple transactions in one sandwich.** Our detection matches the canonical triple: a bot frontrun, a victim, then a backrun, all in the same pool and same block, with the frontrun and backrun from the same sender, the victim from a different sender, and strictly ordered transaction indices. A multi-victim sandwich (one frontrun, several victims, one backrun) currently surfaces as one detected sandwich per victim, deduplicated on the exact frontrun/victim/backrun triple, so every victim is still captured, but we don't yet fold them into a single logical "campaign." Multi-leg frontruns or backruns (a bot splitting its entry or exit across several txs) we also don't stitch together. Both cases make us under-group rather than over-count, and campaign-level grouping is a good improvement to add.

author: dhanush0512
content: **2. Profit when the backrun doesn't fully undo the frontrun.** Extracted value is the attacker's realized net proceeds in the pool's tokens across the frontrun and backrun, priced in USD (stablecoins and WETH directly), minus the attacker's gas, and winsorized to drop decode outliers. When the backrun only partially unwinds, the bot is left holding inventory, so our figure reflects the closed portion and does not mark-to-market the residual position. That is an approximation, and honestly the convention here is a real open question. We'd genuinely value the group's view on whether to count realized-only or also value the leftover inventory.

author: dhanush0512
content: **3. How conservative the estimate is.** We treat the numbers as a lower bound. The main sources of undercount: pool coverage is ~75% (sandwiches in unmapped pools are missed entirely), unknown tokens are priced at 0 rather than estimated (so their USD isn't counted), and we currently cover five DEX families. And you're right that anything more involved is out of scope today: combined sandwich plus arbitrage, JIT liquidity, and cross-pool or cross-block strategies are not detected. So the headline figures are a floor, and the true extent is higher.

author: dhanush0512
content: **4. Victim perspective and % of volume.** Fully agree. We deliberately keep attacker extracted value and victim volume as separate metrics, and we're careful that the victim's actual loss is not the same as the attacker's profit (there are DEX fees and execution inefficiencies in between). Concretely we'll add extracted value as a percentage of the victim's trade volume, which as you say is more meaningful to a user than the absolute amount, plus average per attack. A proper victim-loss figure (slippage against a no-sandwich counterfactual) is a modeling step we'd add carefully rather than conflate with attacker profit.

author: dhanush0512
content:
**5. Pools affected most, and pool size vs extracted value.** We already surface the most-attacked pools and pairs by count and by victim volume. We don't track pool liquidity/TVL yet, so the pool-size versus extraction scatter you suggest is a great addition. It should show the tradeoff nicely: small pools with high slippage but few trades on one end, deep pools with high volume on the other.

**6. Percentage of attacked trades.** Today we report the share of blocks that contain a sandwich. The share of individual swaps attacked, by both count and volume within covered pools, is more informative and we'll add it.

author: dhanush0512
content: **7. Slippage-tolerance cross-check.** Really like this one. Comparing execution price to the transaction's minimum-out or slippage tolerance (a fill at the worst allowed price strongly implies a sandwich) gives us an independent validation of the detection rather than just trusting the pattern match. We'll use it to estimate precision and recall, and it may also help us catch cases the strict triple misses.

author: dhanush0512
content: <@695963554888679485> We'll fold these in and share updates as they land. Thanks again for taking the time.
